newsitem.title: GERMANY: Dell sees Internet sales driving growth.
newsitem.headline: Dell sees Internet sales driving growth.

text.p: Dell Computer Corp. chief executive Michael Dell said on Tuesday he expected the Internet to help the company's European sales grow two to three times faster than the rest of industry over the next few years.
"We are quite excited about the outlook for the industry," he said at a news conference. "We still have very strong targets to grow this (European) business at rates faster than the industry."
Dell's European sales in the first quarter rose to $644 million, up 38 percent, while sales on the continent increased only about 8.4 percent, according to market researcher IDC.
To keep European sales on the rise, Dell last week launched true online commerce systems allowing German and British customers to buy computers over the Internet.
The company would follow with similar capabilities next week in France, and in Scandinavia and the Benelux countries later this summer, Dell said.
"Dell is using the Internet as a major sales channel," he said. "We are driving the Internet very hard."

Since March, Dell has offered European customers an Internet site with a limited number of computers they could order by sending electronic mail messages. The messages then had to be re-keyed into Dell's order processing system.

The new systems allow buyers to select from a full range of software, components and accessories. They display price increases as features are added, offer payment options and deposit order directly into the production que.
"This is true online commerce," said Hans-Juergen Mammitzsch, managing director of Dell Computer GmbH in Langen, Germany.
Dell's Internet sales have been one of the leading examples of the potential of the new medium for direct retail merchants.
In the United States, where Dell has used the Internet for sales for about a year, the global network was generating "far in excess" of $1 million a day, Dell said.

In Germany, the company had online and e-mail sales of about $1 million in May, Mammitzsch said. He expected Internet sales to account for about five percent of the country's total turnover by the end of the year.
Worldwide, Dell also expected sales to outpace the industry as a whole. The company would benefit as Intel Corp. brought out faster processors later this year.
"New processors accelerate the (PC) replacement cycle and bring new buyers into the market," Dell said.

At the same time, Dell expected to boost sales by expanding its product line of servers -- large computers that control networks. It would also add workstations, brawny machines used by scientists and engineers, this year.
